title: Money Maze: Financial Navigator
description: Navigate the maze of financial decisions! Start as a college graduate with your first salary. Make smart choices about saving, investing, taxes, insurance, and EMIs. Watch out for lifestyle inflation traps and market crashes! Can you reach Financial Freedom?
learning_objectives: Understand the basics of personal finance: budgeting, saving, and investing
Learn about Indian tax-saving instruments like Section 80C, PPF, and NPS
Develop smart decision-making around EMIs, credit cards, and loans
Explore how compound interest and SIPs build long-term wealth
Recognize lifestyle inflation traps and the importance of insurance

how_to_play.title: How to Play
steps: Roll the dice to move your token along the 20-tile financial journey board
Land on Financial Decision tiles to face real-life money choices about saving, investing, and spending
Visit Investment Centre tiles to spend your savings on SIPs, Fixed Deposits, or Term Insurance
Face Financial Crisis tiles where you must answer a finance quiz to survive market crashes, tax audits, or loan defaults
Race AI competitors Sonia and Farhan to reach the Financial Freedom finish tile with the highest savings, income, and credit score
tips: Start building your savings early -- compound interest is your best friend over time
Always keep an emergency fund before making risky investments
Use power-ups wisely -- the Tax Shield can save you from a painful audit penalty
Pay attention to your credit score -- it affects your ability to get good loan rates later

evt_emi_decision.title: EMI Temptation: Bike on Loan
evt_emi_decision.story: You just got your first salary of Rs 30,000! A showroom offers a shiny new bike for Rs 1,20,000 with 'easy EMI' of Rs 5,000/month for 24 months. Your friends all have bikes. But Rs 5,000/month is a big chunk of your salary. What do you do?

choices.label: Take the loan -- you deserve it!
choices.feedback: You got the bike, but the EMI eats 16% of your salary every month for 2 years. With interest, you pay Rs 1,44,000 total -- Rs 24,000 extra! Your savings ability is now severely limited. Lesson: EMI makes things look cheap but costs much more over time.

choices.label: Save for 6 months, then buy a used bike
choices.feedback: Smart move! After 6 months of saving Rs 5,000/month, you buy a quality used bike for Rs 50,000 cash. No EMI burden, no interest paid, and your savings habit is established. You still ride to work in style! Lesson: Delayed gratification saves you lakhs over a lifetime.

choices.label: Use Metro/bus for now, invest the difference
choices.feedback: Brilliant long-term thinking! The Rs 5,000/month you would have spent on EMI goes into a SIP instead. In 2 years, your SIP grows to Rs 1,40,000+ with returns. You can then buy the bike outright AND have money left over. Lesson: Investing what you would have paid as EMI builds wealth faster than you think.

evt_emi_decision.reflection_prompt: Think about a time you really wanted something expensive. Did you buy it right away or wait? How did that decision feel a month later? What does this choice tell you about how you handle the tension between wanting something now and planning for the future?

evt_tax_saving.title: Tax Saving Season: Section 80C
evt_tax_saving.story: It is March -- tax saving deadline! Your office HR says you can save up to Rs 1,50,000 under Section 80C to reduce your taxable income. You have not invested anything yet. Your CA suggests PPF, ELSS mutual funds, or NPS. Each has different lock-in periods and returns. What do you choose?

choices.label: Invest Rs 50,000 in ELSS mutual funds (3-year lock-in)
choices.feedback: Excellent choice for a young investor! ELSS funds invest in the stock market and historically return 12-15% per year. The 3-year lock-in is the shortest among 80C options. You save roughly Rs 5,000 in taxes AND your money grows. Lesson: ELSS gives you tax saving + wealth creation in one instrument.

choices.label: Open a PPF account with Rs 50,000 (15-year lock-in)
choices.feedback: Safe and government-backed! PPF currently gives 7.1% annual return, completely tax-free. The 15-year lock-in is long, but the power of compound interest over 15 years is massive. Rs 50,000/year in PPF grows to over Rs 16 lakhs in 15 years. Lesson: PPF is the safest 80C option -- start early and let compounding do the work.

choices.label: Panic-buy a random insurance policy the agent is pushing
choices.feedback: Classic mistake! The agent sold you an endowment policy with high premiums, poor returns (4-5%), and a 20-year lock-in. You get neither good insurance nor good returns. Rs 2,000/month locked away for years. Lesson: Never mix insurance and investment. Buy term insurance for protection and mutual funds for growth -- separately.

evt_insurance_choice.title: Insurance: Protection vs Investment
evt_insurance_choice.story: An insurance agent visits your office and pitches two plans. Plan A is a term insurance policy: Rs 1 crore cover for just Rs 700/month -- pure protection, no money back. Plan B is an endowment plan: Rs 10 lakh cover for Rs 5,000/month, but you get money back after 20 years. Your colleagues all bought Plan B. What do you choose?

choices.label: Buy Term Insurance (Plan A) -- pure protection
choices.feedback: Financial experts agree: term insurance is the smartest choice. You get Rs 1 crore protection for just Rs 700/month. The remaining Rs 4,300 you save (vs Plan B) can go into mutual funds earning 12%+ returns. After 20 years, your SIP of Rs 4,300/month grows to Rs 40+ lakhs -- far more than Plan B's return. Lesson: Keep insurance and investment separate. Term insurance + SIP always beats endowment plans.

choices.label: Buy Endowment Plan (Plan B) -- get money back
choices.feedback: The agent is happy, but your wallet is not. You are paying Rs 5,000/month for only Rs 10 lakh cover (not enough!) and the return after 20 years is roughly 5% -- barely beating inflation. Meanwhile, Rs 5,000/month in an index fund would have given you Rs 50+ lakhs. Lesson: 'Money back' sounds nice but the returns are terrible. Endowment plans are neither good insurance nor good investment.

choices.label: Skip insurance entirely -- you are young and healthy
choices.feedback: Risky gamble! Life is unpredictable. Without term insurance, your family has zero financial protection if something happens to you. A sudden medical emergency could wipe out all your savings. Lesson: Insurance is not optional -- it is the foundation of any financial plan. Get term insurance first, invest later.

evt_stock_market.title: Stock Market Buzz: Hot Tips!
evt_stock_market.story: Your WhatsApp group is buzzing! A friend says 'Buy XYZ stock -- it will double in 3 months!' Another friend made Rs 50,000 last week on penny stocks. You have Rs 20,000 in savings. The market is at an all-time high. Everyone seems to be making easy money. What do you do?

choices.label: Invest all Rs 20,000 in the hot tip stock
choices.feedback: Three months later, the stock crashes 60%. Your Rs 20,000 is now worth Rs 8,000. The friend who recommended it has gone silent. You panic-sell at a loss. Lesson: WhatsApp tips are not investment advice. Hot tips usually mean someone is trying to pump the stock before dumping it. Never invest money you cannot afford to lose.

choices.label: Start a monthly SIP in an index fund instead
choices.feedback: Boring? Maybe. But a Nifty 50 index fund SIP of Rs 3,000/month has historically returned 12-13% per year over 10+ years. You do not need to pick stocks or follow tips. The market goes up and down, but SIP averages your cost over time. After 10 years, your Rs 3.6 lakhs invested becomes roughly Rs 7 lakhs. Lesson: SIP in index funds is the simplest and most proven way to build wealth.

choices.label: Study investing basics first, then invest small
choices.feedback: The wisest approach! You spend a month learning about P/E ratios, company fundamentals, and asset allocation. Then you invest Rs 5,000 in a diversified equity fund as a test. You learn from real experience without risking too much. Lesson: Financial literacy is the highest-return investment you can make. Learn first, earn later.

evt_stock_market.reflection_prompt: Following 'hot tips' from friends can feel exciting, but how do you usually decide whom to trust with important decisions? What is the difference between taking a calculated risk and gambling? How do you build the confidence to go against the crowd when the crowd might be wrong?

evt_credit_card_trap.title: Credit Card Trap: Minimum Due Illusion
evt_credit_card_trap.story: You got your first credit card with a Rs 1,00,000 limit! You go on a shopping spree during the Amazon sale and spend Rs 45,000. The bill arrives. You can pay the full amount, or just the 'minimum due' of Rs 2,250 (5%). Paying minimum due looks so easy and leaves you cash to spend more. What do you do?

choices.label: Pay the full Rs 45,000 bill immediately
choices.feedback: Smart! By paying in full, you owe zero interest. Credit cards charge 36-42% annual interest on unpaid balances -- the highest interest rate of any financial product. Paying full makes the credit card work FOR you (cashback, rewards) instead of against you. Your credit score jumps. Lesson: A credit card is a tool, not free money. Always pay the full bill every month.

choices.label: Pay just the minimum due of Rs 2,250
choices.feedback: Trap activated! The remaining Rs 42,750 now attracts 3.5% interest PER MONTH (42% per year). Next month's bill is Rs 44,246. If you keep paying minimum, it takes over 10 years to clear the debt, and you pay Rs 1,30,000+ in total for a Rs 45,000 purchase! Your credit score drops sharply. Lesson: Minimum due is the bank's way of keeping you in debt forever. It is the most expensive loan you will ever take.

choices.label: Pay Rs 30,000 now, rest next month
choices.feedback: Decent compromise but still costly! Interest applies on the ENTIRE Rs 45,000 from the date of purchase, not just the unpaid Rs 15,000. That is a surprise most people do not know. You end up paying roughly Rs 3,000 in interest. Better than minimum, but full payment is always best. Lesson: Credit card interest is calculated on the total amount if you do not pay in full.

evt_credit_card_trap.reflection_prompt: Credit card minimum payments feel like a relief in the moment but cost much more long-term. Can you think of other situations in life where the 'easy' option now creates a bigger problem later? What strategies help you resist the pull of short-term comfort?

evt_real_estate.title: Real Estate Dream: Buy or Rent?
evt_real_estate.story: Your parents say 'Buying a house is the best investment!' A 2BHK flat costs Rs 50 lakhs. You can get a home loan at 8.5% for 20 years -- EMI will be Rs 43,000/month. Your current rent is Rs 12,000/month. Your salary is Rs 60,000. Should you buy now?

choices.label: Buy the flat -- EMI is like forced savings!
choices.feedback: The EMI is 72% of your salary -- dangerously high! Financial experts say EMI should not exceed 30-40% of income. Over 20 years, you pay Rs 1.03 crore for a Rs 50 lakh flat. You are house-rich but cash-poor -- no money for emergencies, vacations, or other investments. Lesson: A home loan EMI above 40% of income is financial suffocation. Wait until your income grows.

choices.label: Keep renting, invest the EMI difference in SIPs
choices.feedback: Counterintuitive but mathematically smart! Rent is Rs 12,000 vs EMI of Rs 43,000. You invest the Rs 31,000 difference in equity mutual funds. At 12% returns over 20 years, your SIP grows to Rs 3.1 crore -- while the flat's value might be Rs 1.5-2 crore. Plus, you stay flexible and mobile. Lesson: Renting + investing often beats buying, especially when you are young and your rent-to-EMI ratio is very different.

choices.label: Wait 5 years, grow your salary, save for a bigger down payment
choices.feedback: Patient and wise! In 5 years, your salary could double to Rs 1.2 lakhs, making a Rs 43,000 EMI just 36% of income -- much more manageable. A larger down payment also means a smaller loan and less interest paid. Lesson: The best time to buy a house is when you can afford it comfortably, not when society pressures you.

evt_retirement_planning.title: Retirement Planning: Start Now or Later?
evt_retirement_planning.story: You are 23 years old. Your office offers NPS (National Pension System) with employer matching. A colleague says 'Retirement? I will think about it at 40!' But your CA shows you a shocking calculation: investing Rs 5,000/month from age 23 vs age 35 in NPS at 10% returns. What do you decide?

choices.label: Start NPS now with Rs 5,000/month + employer match
choices.feedback: The power of compounding at its finest! Starting at 23, your Rs 5,000/month grows to Rs 3.8 crore by age 60 (37 years). If you wait until 35, the same Rs 5,000/month becomes only Rs 1.1 crore (25 years). That is Rs 2.7 CRORE lost by waiting just 12 years! Plus, NPS gives you extra tax benefits under Section 80CCD(1B). Lesson: Time in the market beats timing the market. Start investing for retirement in your 20s.

choices.label: Start with just Rs 1,000/month in NPS, increase later
choices.feedback: Good start! Even Rs 1,000/month from age 23 grows to Rs 76 lakhs by 60. The habit of investing matters more than the amount initially. You can increase your contribution as your salary grows. Lesson: Do not let the perfect be the enemy of the good. Start small, but START.

choices.label: Skip NPS -- retirement is 37 years away!
choices.feedback: This is exactly what most people do -- and regret at 50. By delaying 12 years, you need to invest Rs 17,000/month to match what Rs 5,000/month would have achieved starting now. That is 3.4x more money from your pocket because you lost 12 years of compounding. Lesson: The most expensive mistake in finance is not starting early. Time is your greatest asset.

evt_upi_digital.title: UPI and Digital Money Management
evt_upi_digital.story: UPI has made spending incredibly easy -- just scan and pay! You notice you have been spending Rs 8,000 more per month since you started using UPI because you do not 'feel' the money leaving. Your bank balance keeps shrinking. Digital payments are convenient but invisible. How do you handle this?

choices.label: Set up a budget app and track every UPI transaction
choices.feedback: Awareness is the first step! By tracking expenses, you discover Rs 3,000/month goes to food delivery apps, Rs 2,000 to impulse online shopping, and Rs 3,000 to subscriptions you forgot about. You cut Rs 5,000/month of wasteful spending. Lesson: What gets measured gets managed. A budget app turns invisible digital spending into visible decisions.

choices.label: Create separate accounts: spending, saving, investing
choices.feedback: The 50-30-20 rule in action! You set up auto-transfers on salary day: 50% to needs account, 30% to wants account, 20% to savings/investment account. Your UPI is linked only to the wants account. When that account hits zero, you stop spending. Simple and effective. Lesson: Automating your money flow removes willpower from the equation. Pay yourself first.

choices.label: UPI is convenient -- keep spending as usual
choices.feedback: Six months later, you have zero savings and a credit card bill building up. The ease of UPI scanning led to Rs 48,000 in unnecessary spending this half-year. Lifestyle inflation is real and silent. Lesson: Convenience without control is a trap. Technology should help you save, not just spend.

evt_boss_market_crash.title: Financial Crisis: Stock Market Crash!
evt_boss_market_crash.story: Breaking news: The stock market crashes 30% in one week! Your mutual fund investments are down Rs 15,000. Your WhatsApp groups are panicking. TV anchors are screaming. Everyone is selling. What is the RIGHT thing to do?

choices.label: Stay calm and continue your SIPs -- buy more at lower prices
choices.feedback: CORRECT! This is exactly what smart investors do. Market crashes are temporary -- every major crash in Indian stock market history has been followed by recovery and new highs. By continuing SIPs during a crash, you buy more units at lower prices, which dramatically boosts returns when the market recovers. The 2008 crash investors who held on made 300%+ returns by 2015. Lesson: Market crashes are sales for long-term investors. Never panic-sell.

choices.label: Sell everything immediately before it falls more!
choices.feedback: WRONG! You just locked in your losses. By selling at the bottom, you turned a temporary paper loss into a permanent real loss. When the market recovers 6 months later (it always does), you are not invested to benefit. Studies show that missing just the 10 best days in the market over 20 years cuts your returns by more than half. Lesson: Panic selling is the number one wealth destroyer. Time in the market beats timing the market.

choices.label: Take a loan to buy more stocks -- they are cheap!
choices.feedback: DANGEROUS! Never borrow money to invest in the stock market. If the market falls further, you lose borrowed money AND have to pay EMI on the loan. This is how people go bankrupt. Only invest money you will not need for 5+ years. Lesson: Leverage (borrowing to invest) amplifies losses just as much as gains. Invest only what you can afford to lose.

challenge.question: The stock market crashes 30% in one week. Your mutual fund investments are down Rs 15,000. What is the RIGHT thing to do?
options: Stay calm and continue your SIPs -- buy more at lower prices
Sell everything immediately before it falls more!
Take a loan to buy more stocks -- they are cheap!
challenge.explanation: Continuing SIPs during a crash means you buy more units at lower prices (rupee-cost averaging). Every major crash in Indian stock market history has been followed by recovery and new highs. The 2008 crash investors who held on made 300%+ returns by 2015. Panic selling locks in losses permanently, and borrowing to invest amplifies risk dangerously.

evt_boss_tax_audit.title: Financial Crisis: Income Tax Notice!
evt_boss_tax_audit.story: You receive a notice from the Income Tax Department! They found a mismatch between your Form 26AS (tax deducted) and your ITR (tax return filed). Panic sets in. The notice asks you to explain why Rs 2,00,000 in freelance income was not declared. What do you know about tax compliance?

choices.label: File a revised return declaring all income, pay the tax with interest
choices.feedback: CORRECT! Filing a revised return and paying the due tax with interest is the legal and smart approach. The penalty for voluntary disclosure is much less than if the IT department catches undeclared income. Interest under Section 234A/B/C is about 1% per month. Being honest with taxes protects your credit score and financial reputation. Lesson: Always declare all income sources. Tax evasion is a criminal offense; tax planning (using 80C, 80D, HRA) is legal and smart.

choices.label: Ignore the notice -- it is probably a mistake
choices.feedback: WRONG! Never ignore an IT notice. The department escalates: first a reminder, then a penalty of 50-200% of the tax due, and in extreme cases, prosecution. Your bank accounts can be frozen. A tax notice is serious business. Lesson: Respond to every tax notice within 30 days. Ignoring it makes a small problem into a catastrophe.

choices.label: Show fake expense receipts to reduce the tax amount
choices.feedback: ILLEGAL AND DISASTROUS! Submitting false documents is tax fraud, punishable with imprisonment of up to 7 years under the Income Tax Act. With digital tracking, the IT department cross-references PAN, Aadhaar, bank statements, and GST records. Fake receipts are caught easily. Lesson: Tax fraud is never worth it. The legal consequences far outweigh any short-term savings.

challenge.question: You receive an Income Tax notice about Rs 2,00,000 in undeclared freelance income. What should you do?
options: File a revised return declaring all income, pay the tax with interest
Ignore the notice -- it is probably a mistake
Show fake expense receipts to reduce the tax amount
challenge.explanation: Filing a revised return with voluntary disclosure attracts much lower penalties (interest under Section 234A/B/C at ~1% per month) compared to being caught. Ignoring notices leads to escalating penalties of 50-200% and possible asset seizure. Submitting false documents is tax fraud punishable with up to 7 years imprisonment. Honest compliance is always the smartest financial strategy.

evt_boss_loan_default.title: Financial Crisis: EMI Default Warning!
evt_boss_loan_default.story: Disaster! You lost your job and have missed 2 EMI payments on your personal loan. The bank sends a warning letter. Your credit score has already dropped from 750 to 620. Penalty interest of 2% per month is now being charged on top of regular interest. What is the best way out?

choices.label: Call the bank immediately and negotiate a restructuring plan
choices.feedback: CORRECT! Banks would rather restructure your loan than declare it an NPA (Non-Performing Asset). You can request: extended tenure (lower EMI), temporary moratorium (pause payments for 3 months), or reduced interest rate. RBI guidelines require banks to offer restructuring to distressed borrowers. Acting quickly shows good faith and protects your credit score from further damage. Lesson: Communication with your bank is critical. A restructured loan is infinitely better than a defaulted one.

choices.label: Take another loan to pay this EMI
choices.feedback: WRONG! This is the classic debt trap. Taking a new loan to pay an old loan creates a spiral: now you have TWO EMIs, usually at even higher interest rates (since your credit score is low). This is how people end up bankrupt. Lesson: Never borrow to repay borrowing. It is a death spiral. Restructure, negotiate, or liquidate assets -- but never layer debt on debt.

choices.label: Stop answering the bank's calls and hope they give up
choices.feedback: TERRIBLE IDEA! The bank will not give up. After 90 days of default, your loan becomes an NPA. The bank can: send recovery agents, file a case in debt recovery tribunal, get a court order to seize your assets, and report to CIBIL making your credit score crash below 500. With a score that low, no bank will give you any loan or credit card for 7 years. Lesson: Running from debt makes everything worse. Face it, negotiate, and rebuild.

challenge.question: You lost your job and missed 2 EMI payments. The bank sends a warning letter. What is the best way out?
options: Call the bank immediately and negotiate a restructuring plan
Take another loan to pay this EMI
Stop answering the bank's calls and hope they give up
challenge.explanation: Banks prefer restructuring loans over declaring them NPAs (Non-Performing Assets). Options include extended tenure, temporary moratorium, or reduced interest rates. RBI guidelines require banks to offer restructuring to distressed borrowers. Taking new loans to pay old ones creates a devastating debt spiral, and ignoring the bank leads to asset seizure, recovery agents, and a credit score below 500 that blocks all future borrowing for 7 years.

evt_diwali_bonus.title: Diwali Bonus Windfall!
evt_diwali_bonus.story: Happy Diwali! Your company gives you a bonus of Rs 25,000. Your friends are planning a Goa trip costing Rs 20,000. Your phone is 3 years old. Your emergency fund has only Rs 10,000. How do you use the bonus wisely?

choices.label: Put Rs 20,000 in emergency fund, Rs 5,000 on a small celebration
choices.feedback: Wise balance! Financial experts say you need 3-6 months of expenses as an emergency fund before anything else. Your emergency fund grows to Rs 30,000 -- almost 2 months of expenses. And you still enjoy Diwali with Rs 5,000 for sweets, gifts, and a nice dinner. Lesson: Emergency fund first, fun second. The peace of mind of knowing you can handle a job loss or medical emergency is priceless.

choices.label: Goa trip with friends -- YOLO!
choices.feedback: Fun trip, but your emergency fund stays dangerously low at Rs 10,000. When your bike breaks down next month and costs Rs 8,000 to repair, you have to put it on your credit card at 42% interest. The Goa photos look great on Instagram, but the credit card debt does not. Lesson: YOLO is not a financial strategy. Build your safety net before your vacation fund.

evt_promotion_bonus.title: Promotion! Salary Hike of 40%
evt_promotion_bonus.story: Congratulations! After 2 years of hard work, you get promoted. Your salary jumps from Rs 60,000 to Rs 84,000 -- a 40% hike! Your mind immediately goes to upgrading: bigger flat, new car, branded clothes. But your CA warns about 'lifestyle inflation' -- the tendency to increase spending whenever income increases. What do you do?

choices.label: Keep lifestyle same, invest 80% of the hike (Rs 19,200/month)
choices.feedback: The wealth-building golden rule! By investing Rs 19,200/month of your Rs 24,000 hike, you let your lifestyle improve slightly (Rs 4,800 extra spending) while building serious wealth. In 10 years at 12% returns, this monthly investment grows to Rs 45 lakhs! Lesson: The secret of every wealthy person: invest your raises, live below your means.

choices.label: Upgrade flat, buy a car on loan, and celebrate!
choices.feedback: Lifestyle inflation strikes! Your new flat rent is Rs 25,000 (up from Rs 12,000), car EMI is Rs 15,000, and spending on eating out doubles. Despite earning Rs 84,000, you now save LESS than when you earned Rs 60,000. The hedonic treadmill means the happiness from upgrades fades in 2 months, but the EMIs last 5 years. Lesson: Lifestyle inflation is the silent killer of wealth. A bigger salary does not guarantee bigger savings.

evt_investment_centre_1.title: First Investment Centre Visit
evt_investment_centre_1.story: Welcome to the Investment Centre! You have some savings and want to start building wealth. A financial advisor explains three options suited for beginners. Each has different risk levels, lock-in periods, and expected returns.

choices.label: Browse the investment options
choices.feedback: Take your time to understand each option. Good investors research before committing money.

evt_investment_centre_2.title: Advanced Investment Centre
evt_investment_centre_2.story: You are back at the Investment Centre! With more experience now, the advisor shows you advanced options: increasing your SIP amount, exploring NPS for additional tax benefits under 80CCD(1B), or diversifying into gold bonds.

choices.label: Browse the advanced options
choices.feedback: As your income grows, so should your investment strategy. Diversification is the key to managing risk.

win_conditions.description: Reach the Financial Freedom tile! Your success is measured by total savings accumulated, monthly income growth, credit score health, and financial knowledge gained throughout the journey.

glossary_terms.definition: Equated Monthly Installment -- a fixed payment amount you make to the bank every month to repay a loan. It includes both principal (the actual loan amount) and interest (the bank's fee for lending).
glossary_terms.example: A Rs 5,00,000 car loan at 9% for 5 years means an EMI of approximately Rs 10,400/month. Total paid: Rs 6,24,000 -- that is Rs 1,24,000 in interest alone!
glossary_terms.remember_tip: EMI = Every Month I pay -- make sure you can afford it before signing up.

glossary_terms.definition: Systematic Investment Plan -- a method of investing a fixed amount in mutual funds at regular intervals (usually monthly). SIP uses rupee-cost averaging to reduce the impact of market volatility.
glossary_terms.example: A SIP of Rs 5,000/month in an equity mutual fund at 12% annual returns grows to Rs 50 lakhs in 20 years. Total invested: Rs 12 lakhs. Gain: Rs 38 lakhs from compound interest!
glossary_terms.remember_tip: SIP = Small Investments Prosper -- tiny drops fill the ocean over time.

glossary_terms.definition: A 3-digit number (300-900) maintained by CIBIL in India that reflects your creditworthiness. Banks check this score before approving loans or credit cards. 750+ is considered good.
glossary_terms.example: With a credit score of 800, you get a home loan at 8.5%. With a score of 600, the same loan costs 11% -- that is Rs 8 lakhs more in interest over 20 years!
glossary_terms.remember_tip: Credit Score = your financial report card. Pay bills on time to keep it above 750.

glossary_terms.definition: A section of the Indian Income Tax Act that allows you to reduce your taxable income by up to Rs 1,50,000 per year by investing in specific instruments like PPF, ELSS, NPS, life insurance premiums, and tuition fees.
glossary_terms.example: If your taxable income is Rs 8,00,000 and you invest Rs 1,50,000 under 80C, you are taxed on only Rs 6,50,000 -- saving you roughly Rs 30,000 in taxes (at 20% slab).
glossary_terms.remember_tip: 80C = 80% of your tax-saving headaches solved in one section. Use it fully every year!

glossary_terms.definition: Interest calculated on both the initial principal and the accumulated interest from previous periods. Often called the 'eighth wonder of the world' because it makes money grow exponentially over time.
glossary_terms.example: Rs 1,00,000 at 10% simple interest for 30 years = Rs 4,00,000. The same amount at 10% compound interest for 30 years = Rs 17,45,000. That is 4x more from compounding!
glossary_terms.remember_tip: Compound Interest = your money making babies, and those babies making babies. Start early!

compound_interest.definition: Interest earned on both the initial principal and the accumulated interest from previous periods. The "eighth wonder of the world."
compound_interest.example: $1,000 at 10% compounded annually becomes $1,100 after year 1, then $1,210 after year 2.
compound_interest.real_world_example: Warren Buffett started investing at age 11. Compound interest turned his early investments into billions.

diversification.definition: Spreading investments across different assets to reduce risk. "Don't put all your eggs in one basket."
diversification.example: Instead of buying only tech stocks, investing in stocks, bonds, and real estate.
diversification.real_world_example: Index funds like the S&P 500 automatically diversify across 500 companies.

inflation.definition: The rate at which the general level of prices for goods and services rises, reducing purchasing power over time.
inflation.example: If inflation is 3%, something that costs ₹100 today will cost ₹103 next year.
inflation.real_world_example: In 1950, a movie ticket cost about ₹1. Today it costs ₹200+ — that's inflation over decades.

budgeting.definition: Creating a plan for how to spend and save money. The 50/30/20 rule suggests 50% needs, 30% wants, 20% savings.
budgeting.example: Tracking monthly income of ₹50,000: ₹25,000 rent/food, ₹15,000 entertainment, ₹10,000 savings.
budgeting.real_world_example: YNAB (You Need A Budget) helped millions of users save an average of $600 in their first two months.

assets_liabilities.definition: Assets put money in your pocket (investments, property). Liabilities take money out (loans, credit card debt).
assets_liabilities.example: A rental property generating rent is an asset. A car loan with monthly payments is a liability.
assets_liabilities.real_world_example: Robert Kiyosaki's Rich Dad Poor Dad popularized this distinction, changing how millions think about money.

emergency_fund.definition: Money set aside to cover unexpected expenses like medical bills or job loss. Experts recommend 3-6 months of living expenses.
emergency_fund.example: Saving ₹10,000 monthly until you have ₹1,80,000 set aside for emergencies.
emergency_fund.real_world_example: During COVID-19, people with emergency funds could weather job losses without going into debt.

roi.definition: A measure of the profitability of an investment, calculated as (Gain - Cost) / Cost × 100%.
roi.real_world_example: Education has one of the highest ROIs — college graduates earn 80% more than those with only high school diplomas.

tax_planning.definition: Legally minimizing tax liability through smart financial decisions like deductions, exemptions, and tax-advantaged accounts.
tax_planning.example: Investing in ELSS mutual funds to save up to ₹46,800 in taxes under Section 80C.
tax_planning.real_world_example: Companies like Apple use international tax planning to significantly reduce their effective tax rates.

cultural_context: Personal finance education is largely absent from India's formal school curriculum, leaving many young adults unprepared for the financial decisions of adult life. This game builds the foundational money-management instincts that schools rarely teach.
